questions.stem: Which is a description of land use rather than land cover?
options: A market garden producing vegetables for city shops
A stand of eucalypt forest on the slopes of a hill
A seasonal wetland on the floodplain of a river
A native grassland on a flat basalt plain west of the city
questions.explanation: Land use describes how people use the land, such as for farming, housing or recreation. Forest, wetland and grassland describe what physically covers the land, which is land cover.

questions.stem: Greenfield development is best defined as:
options: replacing existing houses in established suburbs with townhouses and apartments
planting trees and creating parks on land that was once used for housing, industry or other urban purposes
building on land not previously developed for urban use, usually farmland on the urban fringe
redeveloping former industrial land, such as old factories and rail yards, for housing
questions.explanation: Greenfield sites have not been built on before, so development usually means converting farmland at the edge of a city or town. Redeveloping former industrial land is brownfield development.

questions.stem: Melbourne's Docklands, built on former port and railway land beside the central city, is an example of:
options: rural depopulation
a green wedge on the urban fringe
brownfield redevelopment
greenfield development
questions.explanation: Brownfield redevelopment reuses land that has previously been developed, often former industrial or transport land, for new uses such as housing and offices. Greenfield development is on land never before built on.

questions.stem: In a middle-ring suburb, a single house on a 700 m² block is demolished and replaced with three townhouses. This process is best described as:
options: urban consolidation through infill development
urban sprawl through greenfield development
brownfield redevelopment of former industrial land
rural-to-urban fringe development
questions.explanation: Urban consolidation increases the number of dwellings within an existing urban area, here by subdividing one block for three homes. Sprawl and greenfield development extend the city outward onto undeveloped land.

questions.stem: Older workers' cottages in an inner suburb are renovated by higher-income newcomers, property values and rents rise, and many lower-income renters move away. This process is called:
options: greenfield development
suburbanisation
gentrification
urban sprawl
questions.explanation: Gentrification is the renewal of older housing by wealthier residents, which changes the social character of an area and often displaces lower-income residents. Urban sprawl and suburbanisation describe outward growth of the city.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the main stages of greenfield development on a city's fringe?
options: Rezoning of farmland, then subdivision and servicing, then house building, then residents arrive
House building, then rezoning of farmland, then subdivision and servicing, then residents arrive
Subdivision and servicing, then residents arrive, then rezoning, then house building
Residents arrive, then rezoning of farmland, then house building, then subdivision and servicing
questions.explanation: Land must first be rezoned to allow urban use; it is then subdivided into lots with roads, water, sewerage and power before houses are built and occupied. Houses cannot lawfully be built before the land is zoned and subdivided for housing.

questions.stem: When a geographer describes the scale of a land use change, they are describing:
options: whether the change has positive or negative impacts
the reasons that individuals and groups gave for supporting the change
the size of the area affected, from local to regional or national
the order in which the stages of the change took place
questions.explanation: Observational scale refers to the size of the area being studied, such as a single site, a suburb, a region or a nation. The order of stages is the time sequence of change, which is a separate part of the process.

questions.stem: Which land use change is at a local scale?
options: The expansion of irrigated cropping across the whole of the Murray–Darling Basin
A national shift in farming from sheep grazing to cropping over several decades
The worldwide conversion of tropical forest to pasture and plantations
The rezoning of a 40-hectare block of farmland on the edge of a country town
questions.explanation: A 40-hectare block on the edge of one town is a local-scale change of the kind studied in fieldwork. A river basin is regional, a national trend is national, and worldwide conversion is global.

questions.stem: A growth area is planned on flat, cleared farmland beside an existing railway line on a city's fringe. Which geographic characteristics best explain why this site was chosen?
options: Forested land provides shade, and clearing it supplies timber for house building
Flood-prone land is fertile, so residents can grow much of their own food in large gardens
Flat land is cheap to subdivide and service, and the railway links residents to jobs
Steep land drains well, and the distance from transport keeps the estate quiet
questions.explanation: Flat, already cleared land keeps the cost of roads, drainage and building low, and an existing rail line gives access to employment and services. The site described is neither steep, forested nor flood-prone.

questions.stem: Melbourne's urban growth boundary is:
options: the limit beyond which the Commonwealth government does not fund any new public transport
a line set by the state government separating land for urban growth from non-urban land
the boundary of the City of Melbourne local government area in the central city
a ring road built to carry freight traffic around the edge of the metropolitan area
questions.explanation: The urban growth boundary marks where urban development can occur, protecting land beyond it, such as green wedges and farmland, from subdivision. Moving it requires a state government decision.

questions.stem: Melbourne's green wedges are:
options: strips of parkland planted along every new freeway built in the growth corridors
inner-city areas set aside for high-density apartment development near rail stations
former industrial sites that must be planted with trees before they can be redeveloped for housing
non-urban areas outside the growth boundary, kept for farming, conservation and recreation
questions.explanation: Green wedges are the non-urban lands between and beyond the growth corridors, protected for uses such as agriculture, water catchments, conservation and recreation. They are not freeway landscaping or brownfield sites.

questions.stem: In Victoria's growth areas, a precinct structure plan sets out:
options: the names of the families who are allowed to buy land in the new community
the number of trees that each household must plant in its garden each year
where housing, town centres, schools, roads and open space will go in a new community
the price at which each house in a new estate must be sold to its first buyer
questions.explanation: Precinct structure plans, prepared by the Victorian Planning Authority with councils, set out the future land uses and infrastructure of a new community before development begins. They do not fix house prices or choose buyers.

questions.stem: In a Victorian planning scheme, zones are used to:
options: control which land uses and developments are allowed on each piece of land
set the council rates that each property owner must pay every year
record the names of the owners of every property in the municipality
decide which government schools the children in each street are allowed to attend
questions.explanation: Each planning scheme divides land into zones, such as residential, industrial, farming or green wedge zones, and each zone sets the uses that are allowed, need a permit or are prohibited. Rates and land titles are handled by other systems.

questions.stem: In Victoria, most applications for a planning permit are decided by:
options: the Commonwealth Parliament
the High Court of Australia
the local council, as the responsible authority
the Australian Bureau of Statistics
questions.explanation: Councils administer the planning scheme for their municipality and decide most permit applications. The Australian Bureau of Statistics collects data and has no planning role.

questions.stem: A resident objects to a council's decision to approve a six-storey apartment building in their street. The usual body that can review the council's decision is:
options: the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA)
the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT)
the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)
the Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC)
questions.explanation: VCAT reviews planning decisions when applicants or objectors challenge a council's decision, and it can confirm, change or overturn it. The other bodies have no role in planning appeals.

questions.stem: Under Victoria's Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006, a cultural heritage management plan is required before some high-impact developments in areas of cultural heritage sensitivity. This shows that land use change can be influenced by:
options: the views of residents living in other states and territories of Australia
legislation and organisations protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage
the personal preferences of the developer's architects and builders
the market price of the land at the time of sale
questions.explanation: The Act requires assessment, often with the relevant Registered Aboriginal Party, before certain developments proceed, which can change where and how land is developed. This is the influence of legislation and organisations rather than of market price or individual preference.

questions.stem: A rural district's farmland is being converted to a large solar farm. Which reason for this change is linked to the geographical characteristics of the area?
options: The decision of one landholder to retire and lease the land to an energy company
High solar radiation, flat land and a nearby high-voltage transmission line
A national target for renewable energy set by the Commonwealth government
A rise in the price that energy companies pay for electricity generated
questions.explanation: Sunshine, flat terrain and access to the electricity grid are characteristics of the place that make it suitable for solar generation. Targets, prices and a landholder's decision are reasons too, but they are policy, economic and individual influences rather than geographical characteristics.

questions.stem: Developers, councils, state government agencies and community groups all took part in a land use change. Studying the influence of each is part of investigating the:
options: location of the area
reasons for change
time sequence of change
scale of change
questions.explanation: The study design lists the influence of individuals, organisations and planning strategies among the reasons for land use change. The time sequence concerns when the stages happened, not who caused them.

questions.stem: The interconnection of a new housing estate with its surrounding region is best shown by:
options: the colour of the roof tiles chosen for the display homes at the estate's entrance
the number of bedrooms in the most common type of house built in the estate
the street names chosen by the developer for each stage of the new estate
residents travelling to jobs and services elsewhere in the metropolitan area by road and rail
questions.explanation: Interconnection concerns the links between places, such as flows of people, goods and water. Commuting to jobs and services connects the estate to the wider region, whereas roof colour and street names are internal characteristics.

questions.stem: A new estate's stormwater drains into a creek that flows through three older suburbs to the bay. After the estate is built, residents downstream report more frequent flooding. This best illustrates:
options: a temporal distribution, as flooding happens only at one time of year in the area
a change in absolute location, as the creek has moved to a new set of coordinates
an interconnection, as change in one place has impacts in the surrounding region
a spatial association, as the estate and the older suburbs have similar land uses
questions.explanation: The creek links the estate to places downstream, so increased runoff from new roofs and roads affects other suburbs. Spatial association compares two distributions; it does not describe a flow from one place to another.

questions.stem: Replacing paddocks with roofs, roads and car parks is likely to change local hydrology by:
options: reducing flash flooding because drains remove water from the area
reducing the pollutants carried into creeks after heavy rain
increasing the volume and speed of stormwater runoff into creeks
increasing the amount of rainwater that soaks into the soil
questions.explanation: Impervious surfaces stop water soaking in, so more rain runs off, faster, carrying litter, oil and sediment into creeks. Drains speed the water away from the estate but deliver it to waterways more quickly, raising flood peaks downstream.

questions.stem: Suburbs with little vegetation and many dark roofs and roads are often several degrees hotter on summer afternoons than nearby parkland. This is called:
options: the enhanced greenhouse effect
the rain shadow effect
the ice–albedo effect
the urban heat island effect
questions.explanation: Dark, hard surfaces absorb and store heat and there is less evaporative cooling from plants, so built-up areas are warmer than their surroundings. The enhanced greenhouse effect warms the whole planet rather than particular suburbs.

questions.stem: Which is a negative economic impact on the surrounding region of housing replacing market gardens on a city's fringe?
options: The construction jobs created while roads, services and houses are being built
The increase in council rate revenue from the new households moving into the area
The new shops and businesses that open to serve the residents of the estate
The loss of productive farmland close to city markets, raising transport costs for fresh food
questions.explanation: Fringe farmland is close to markets, so losing it can push production further away and increase transport costs. Construction jobs, rate revenue and new businesses are positive economic impacts.

questions.stem: A survey of 120 households in a new fringe estate finds that 82% of workers commute more than 45 minutes, 70% of households own two or more cars, and the nearest train station is 9 km away. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Residents prefer to drive, so building public transport to the estate would not change their travel
Most residents work within walking distance of their homes, so traffic will not increase in the area
The estate is well served by rail, because a 9 km trip to a station is a short journey by train
Housing has run ahead of public transport, leaving residents dependent on cars for long commutes
questions.explanation: Long commutes, high car ownership and a distant station suggest that transport infrastructure has lagged behind housing, a common social impact in new estates. The data say nothing about whether residents would use transport if it were provided, so a preference cannot be concluded.

questions.stem: An argument for urban consolidation rather than fringe growth is that consolidation:
options: makes more use of existing infrastructure such as rail lines, schools and water mains
always increases the area of backyards and tree canopy in established suburbs
spreads the population over a larger area, reducing traffic on local roads
converts more farmland to housing, increasing the supply of cheap land
questions.explanation: Adding dwellings in established areas uses services that already exist and reduces pressure to expand onto farmland. It usually reduces private open space and canopy rather than increasing them, which is one of its negative impacts.

questions.stem: Which is a positive environmental impact of redeveloping a contaminated former industrial site for housing and parks?
options: The site's soils become more fertile than nearby farmland once housing is built
The site produces more food than it did when it was used for industry
Contaminated soil is cleaned up and the city's demand for fringe farmland is reduced
The number of cars in the area falls to zero once residents move into the site
questions.explanation: Brownfield redevelopment usually requires remediation of contaminated land, and housing people on existing urban land reduces pressure to clear land on the fringe. Housing does not make soil more fertile or produce food.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the impacts of a large greenfield estate replacing grazing land?
options: Its impacts cannot be evaluated, because land use change affects only the land that is being built on
It provides more affordable housing and jobs, but adds runoff, habitat loss and car dependence
It has only positive impacts, because grazing land has no environmental or economic value
It has only negative impacts, because new housing never meets any social or economic need
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation weighs positive impacts, such as housing supply and employment, against negative ones, such as stormwater, loss of habitat and transport problems. Impacts also extend to the surrounding region, so they can and should be evaluated beyond the site.

questions.stem: Which is the most suitable research question for a fieldwork investigation of local land use change?
options: What is the population of Victoria and how has it changed since Federation in 1901?
Is urban growth good or bad for the people of Melbourne and the rest of Australia?
Why do people prefer to buy brand-new houses rather than older ones in established suburbs?
How has the conversion of farmland to housing at Lakeview changed stormwater runoff into Reed Creek?
questions.explanation: A good research question is focused on a local change, names a place and can be answered with primary and secondary data. A question asking whether growth is 'good or bad' is a value judgement that fieldwork cannot test.

questions.stem: In a fieldwork report, the hypothesis is:
options: a description of the limitations of the techniques used in the field
a brief expected answer to the research question, with a justification
a list of the primary and secondary sources used to collect data
a summary of what was learnt, written after the data have been analysed
questions.explanation: The definition of topic includes the research question, its geographic context and a hypothesis with a justification. Limitations belong in the evaluation and a summary of findings belongs in the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which is a primary data source for a fieldwork investigation?
options: A council planning report describing the stages of the estate's development
A land use survey recorded by the student at sites located with a GNSS receiver
Census data on dwellings in the suburb downloaded from the Australian Bureau of Statistics
Historical aerial photographs of the area obtained from a state government website
questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator in the field. Census data, archived photographs and council reports were collected by others, so they are secondary sources.

questions.stem: In the fieldwork for this unit, a GNSS receiver is used mainly to:
options: photograph the area from above so that land use can be compared over time
record the coordinates of each site where primary data were collected so they can be mapped
measure the volume of stormwater flowing through each drain on the new estate
count the number of people living in each dwelling in the area being studied
questions.explanation: GNSS gives the precise location of each observation, which allows the primary data to be mapped and analysed in GIS. Images from above come from aerial photography or satellites, not a GNSS receiver.

questions.stem: Which secondary source would best show the time sequence of land use change in a suburb?
options: An interview with one resident who has lived in the suburb for the past year
A street directory published last year showing the current names of the roads
A series of aerial photographs or satellite images of the suburb taken at intervals over several decades
A single satellite image of the suburb taken on the day the fieldwork was carried out
questions.explanation: Images of the same area at intervals show what changed and when, revealing the sequence of change. A single recent image or a recent directory shows only the present.

questions.stem: A student walks a straight 2 km line outward from a suburban shopping centre, recording land use every 100 m. This fieldwork technique is a:
options: field sketch
population pyramid
transect
choropleth map
questions.explanation: A transect records changes along a line, here showing how land use changes with distance from the centre. A field sketch represents a view from one vantage point rather than a line of observations.

questions.stem: To find residents' views of a new shopping centre, a student surveys 10 people at one bus stop at 2 pm on a weekday. What is the main weakness of this survey?
options: Bus stops are private property, so the student needed a permit from the council to survey
Ten people is too many to survey in one afternoon, so the answers will be unreliable
The small sample at one place and time is unlikely to represent the views of residents generally
Surveys collect only secondary data, so the results cannot be used anywhere in the fieldwork report
questions.explanation: Sample size, location and timing all affect whether results are representative; people at a bus stop on a weekday afternoon may differ from workers or drivers. A survey conducted by the student is primary, not secondary, data.

questions.stem: A developer's brochure says a new estate will 'enhance the natural environment'. When using it as a secondary source, a student should:
options: quote it as the main evidence, because it is the most recent source available
recognise that it may be biased and check its claims against independent data
accept its claims, because developers must publish only verified information
ignore all secondary sources, because only primary data can be used
questions.explanation: Assessing the validity and reliability of sources includes considering who produced them and why; a developer has an interest in presenting the estate favourably. Secondary sources are required in the report, so they should be checked rather than ignored.

questions.stem: In a fieldwork report, the evaluation section considers:
options: the bibliography and the acknowledgement of people who helped with the fieldwork
the limitations of the techniques and sources used, and possibilities for further investigation
the research question, the geographic context of the topic and the hypothesis that is being tested by the investigation
the processed data presented in maps, graphs and tables with correct sourcing
questions.explanation: The evaluation reflects on the relative effectiveness of techniques and sources and suggests future possibilities. The research question and hypothesis belong in the definition of topic.

questions.stem: In GIS, a planner overlays a layer showing land subject to flooding on a layer of proposed housing lots. This allows the planner to:
options: record the exact date on which each house will be completed
measure the air temperature on each of the lots on a hot summer afternoon
identify lots at risk of flooding before the land is subdivided
calculate how many people will buy each lot when it is sold
questions.explanation: Overlaying layers reveals spatial relationships, here where proposed lots coincide with flood-prone land, so plans can be changed before development. Sales and completion dates are not spatial layers of this kind.

questions.stem: Two satellite images of an area taken 15 years apart show vegetated land falling from 70% to 25% of the area. Which statement correctly describes the change?
options: A fall of 180%, because 45 divided by 25 is 1.8 times the area of the remaining vegetation
A fall of 45 percentage points, which is about 64% of the original vegetated land
A fall of 45%, because 70 − 25 = 45 and the answer is a percentage of the area
A fall of about 36%, because 25 divided by 70 is about 0.36 of the original
questions.explanation: Subtracting the two shares gives a change in percentage points (70 − 25 = 45). As a proportion of the original vegetated land, the fall is 45 ÷ 70 ≈ 0.64, or about 64%; 25 ÷ 70 is the share that remains, not the share lost.

questions.stem: On a 1:25 000 topographic map, two points are 8 cm apart. What is the distance between them on the ground?
options: 2 km
20 km
0.2 km
200 km
questions.explanation: Each centimetre on the map represents 25 000 cm, or 250 m, on the ground, so 8 cm represents 8 × 250 m = 2000 m, which is 2 km. Twenty kilometres comes from a slip of one place in converting centimetres.

questions.stem: On a 1:50 000 topographic map with a 1 km grid, a new estate covers about three and a half grid squares. Its approximate area is:
options: 3.5 km², or 350 hectares
35 km², or 3500 hectares
0.35 km², or 35 hectares
175 km², or 17 500 hectares
questions.explanation: Each grid square on a 1 km grid is 1 km², and 1 km² is 100 hectares, so 3.5 squares is 3.5 km² or 350 hectares. Multiplying by 50 from the map scale gives 175, which confuses the scale with the grid.

questions.stem: Census data show that the number of dwellings in a hypothetical suburb rose from 4000 to 6400 between two census years. What was the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 6400 − 4000 = 2400, and 2400 ÷ 4000 = 0.6, or 60%. Dividing the increase by the later figure (2400 ÷ 6400) gives 37.5%, which is the wrong base.

questions.stem: In the six-figure grid reference 452318, the first three digits give the:
options: northing, read up the map from south to north
height of the feature in metres above sea level
number of the map sheet in the state series
easting, read across the map from west to east
questions.explanation: Grid references give the easting first, then the northing. Here 45 is the grid line and 2 is two-tenths of the way across the square to the east.

questions.stem: Which compass direction lies exactly halfway between north-east and east?
options: North-north-east
East-south-east
South-south-east
East-north-east
questions.explanation: On the sixteen-point compass, east-north-east lies between north-east and east. North-north-east lies between north and north-east.

questions.stem: A choropleth map shades each suburb by its percentage change in dwellings between two census years. It is most useful for:
options: measuring the distance from each dwelling to the city
comparing the rate of housing growth between suburbs
showing the exact location of every new dwelling built
showing how the number of dwellings changed each month
questions.explanation: A choropleth map shades whole areas by a value, which makes patterns across areas easy to compare. It cannot show individual dwellings, because every location within a suburb receives the same shade.
